passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel cognitive training program on working memory in adults aged 25–45. The study enrolled 120 participants who were randomly assigned to one of four groups: a control group that received no intervention, and three experimental groups (A, B, and C) that each received a different version of the training program. Baseline working‑memory scores were obtained using the Digit Span subtest of the WAIS‑IV. After a 12‑week intervention period, post‑intervention scores were collected. The researchers aimed to determine which training version produced the greatest absolute improvement and to assess the overall efficacy of the program across all experimental groups. The data are summarized in Table 1 below. The investigators plan to use these results to inform future large‑scale trials and to refine the training protocol for broader clinical application.
stem: Which group had the greatest absolute improvement in working‑memory score?
explanation: Absolute improvement is calculated as Post‑Intervention Score minus Baseline Score. The improvements are: Control +2, Group A +12, Group B +13, Group C +15. Group C shows the largest absolute improvement of +15 points.
trap: A common mistake is to assume the control group’s improvement is the benchmark, overlooking the larger gains in experimental groups.

stem: Which study design best tests the causal effect of the training program?
explanation: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) is the gold standard for establishing causality because random assignment balances known and unknown confounders across groups.
trap: Choosing a cohort or case‑control design overlooks the necessity of randomization to infer causality.

stem: What is the average absolute improvement across all four groups?
explanation: Improvements: Control +2, Group A +12, Group B +13, Group C +15. Sum = 42; average = 42 / 4 = 10.5 points.
trap: Students often add baseline scores instead of differences, leading to inflated totals.

stem: Baseline scores in Table 1 differ among the groups (65 to 70). Why is comparing post-intervention scores alone a poor way to compare how much each group improved?

options.A: Post-intervention scores were not collected for the control group
options.B: All four groups had identical baseline scores, so post scores are redundant
options.C: Groups started at different levels, so change from baseline is needed to compare improvement
options.D: The Digit Span test cannot yield numerical scores

explanation: Correct: Baselines were 70, 68, 65 and 70, so final scores partly reflect starting level; the change from baseline (2, 12, 13, 15) is the appropriate measure of improvement. Why the others are wrong: A) The control group has a post-intervention score of 72 in Table 1. B) Baselines are not identical (68, 65 and 70 differ). D) The Digit Span subtest produces numerical scores, as shown in the table.
trap: Assuming a higher final score always means greater improvement, ignoring different starting points.

stem: After accounting for the change in the control group (practice effect), what is the net improvement attributable to the training in Group C?
explanation: Group C improved by 85 - 70 = 15 points while the control improved by 2 points from repeat testing; net improvement = 15 - 2 = 13 points.
trap: Reporting the raw 15-point gain ignores the practice effect seen in the control group.
